claims.text: High-entropy alloys exhibit an unusually high dynamic strength–ductility synergy.
The strength–ductility synergy is governed by the spatial and temporal interplay between deformation twinning and dislocation slip.
Atomic-scale compositional heterogeneities produce a broad distribution of local stacking-fault energies.
Standard-processed single-crystalline CoCrFeNi preserves inherent atomic-scale chemical heterogeneity.
A homogenization heat treatment can reduce local compositional fluctuations and local stacking-fault-energy variations in CoCrFeNi nanopillars.
Heat-treated and untreated nanopillars can differ only in their degree of atomic-scale chemical heterogeneity.
Local variations in generalized stacking-fault energy mediate the activation of deformation twinning versus dislocation slip.
In chemically heterogeneous CoCrFeNi nanopillars, twinning and dislocation slip activate jointly and/or sequentially during tensile deformation.
Coordinated twinning and slip promote deformation delocalization and delay necking.
Delayed localization and necking enable simultaneous high flow strength and large tensile ductility.
Reducing chemical heterogeneity by homogenization will diminish the synergistic coordination of twinning and slip.
Untreated heterogeneous nanopillars will exhibit greater uniform tensile ductility than homogenized nanopillars.
Untreated heterogeneous nanopillars may exhibit greater work hardening than homogenized nanopillars.
Untreated single-crystalline CoCrFeNi nanopillars can exhibit high room-temperature flow stress together with very high uniform elongation.
The proposed mechanism should hold at room temperature in nanoscale, single-crystalline CoCrFeNi tensile specimens.
The proposed mechanism should apply generally to compositionally complex high-entropy alloys under dynamic tensile conditions.
The cited CoCrFeNi nanopillars reached approximately 110% uniform elongation at flow stresses of 0.6–1.0 GPa.

contradictions.description: The intervention and baseline identify the untreated native-heterogeneity specimen as the control/baseline, whereas the predicted outcome calls the homogenized specimen the control. The intended comparison is clear, but the control designation is internally inconsistent.
